title: America’s grand strategy for a multipolar world
gist: Thomas Graham (Council on Foreign Relations) argues that containment and integration are both obsolete because the US can neither dominate nor transform China and Russia, and proposes 'competitive co-existence': accepting permanent rivalry, rivals' legitimate interests and regime diversity, pursuing incremental advantage, keeping the system genuinely multipolar (preventing a China–Russia–Iran–North Korea bloc from ossifying), and redefining moral leadership as protecting the space for democracy and markets.

insights.claim: Containment and integration, the two US grand strategies since 1945, are inadequate because both assume the US can isolate or reform rival powers into partners in a US-led order, and neither China nor Russia is about to submit.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: Expect a durable multipolar order with persistent great-power friction, not convergence.

insights.claim: Competitive co-existence treats rivalry as a permanent feature to be managed, accepts limits on US power, avoids great-power war given modern weaponry, and leaves space for cooperation on transnational issues like climate change and nuclear proliferation.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: A US policy shift toward managed rivalry would lower tail risk of great-power war.

insights.claim: Graham argues the US should accept other major powers as they are, not challenge the legitimacy of their leaders, and accept that they have legitimate interests it can accommodate where its own goals are not jeopardised.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
insights.so_what: Implies more deal-making with Moscow and Beijing and less regime-change rhetoric.
